Radar, machine learning, and cartography.

About me

I’m a Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation Postdoctoral Fellow and a UW Data Science Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Washington, working with David Shean.

I earned my Ph.D. in Civil and Environmental Engineering at UW in 2025, where my dissertation focused on improving synthetic aperture radar measurements of surface movement and snow depth in mountain environments. I received my B.A. in Geology and Biology from Middlebury College in 2020.

Alongside my academic work, this site brings together my cartography and mountain photography.

Research

I study how snow, ice, and terrain change in mountain environments, and what those changes mean for water resources and natural hazards. My work combines satellite observations, machine learning, and geophysical methods to measure processes that are difficult to observe on the ground.

01 / Surface movement

Radar observations of changing terrain

I use interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) and feature tracking to measure the movement of rock glaciers, landslides, and moraine dams. I develop methods to separate subtle surface motion from atmospheric noise, making satellite radar observations more useful in steep mountain terrain.

02 / Snow

Snow depth from remote sensing

I combine satellite observations and airborne lidar measurements to train machine learning models that estimate snow depth across the western United States. I’m interested in resolving both local snow patterns and regional changes in this seasonal water resource.

The map at the top of this page uses deep-snow to predict snow depth across the North Cascades, including Mount Baker and Mount Shuksan. It is generated daily from remote sensing data, shown over a Copernicus DEM GLO-30 hillshade.

03 / Mountain hazards

From measurements to hazard assessment

I study the degradation of ice-cored moraine dams in Nepal to provide information for glacial lake outburst flood hazard assessments. Across my research, I emphasize uncertainty: understanding where measurements are reliable and which questions they can reasonably answer.

Teaching &
mentorship

I want students to develop an understanding of natural processes through experimentation. My teaching combines discussion, interactive coding, and field-based learning. Jupyter notebooks let students connect equations, code, maps, and observations while building scientific computing skills.

I also emphasize writing and presentation as part of doing science. In teaching and mentorship, I value clear expectations, open communication, and practical support for students with different backgrounds and levels of experience.

2026 / University of Washington

Geospatial Data Analysis

Instructor of record for a combined graduate and undergraduate course with 19 students. Previously a teaching assistant in 2024 and 2025, and a contributor to course development.

2026 / Juneau Icefield Research Program

Research in the field

Led a research project with eight undergraduates evaluating the first NISAR glacier velocity measurements of the Juneau Icefield; taught remote sensing lectures to 31 students and led small-group technical workshops.

Mentorship & workshops

Learning through research and software

I have led GitHub Actions tutorials at SciPy and US-RSE and projects at NASA Earth Sciences / UW and GeoSmart hackweeks.
